\chapter{Eight More Verbs}
\label{ch:la-more-core-verbs}

\section[cōgitō, cōgitāre]{cōgitō — thinking as driving things together}

\label{lesson:LA-C38-cogito}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Sciō} is knowing a fact you already hold. This verb is the work you do before you hold it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: cōgitō — \textquotedblleft{}I think\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Cōgitō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I think},\textquotedblright{} in the sense of turning something over. The dictionary form is \textbf{cōgitāre}. Both \emph{o}-vowels are long and the \emph{g} is hard: \emph{KOH-ghee-TAH-reh}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{cōgitō} — I think
  \item \textbf{cōgitās} — you think, to one person
  \item \textbf{cōgitat} — he thinks, she thinks
  \item \textbf{cōgitāmus} — we think
  \item \textbf{cōgitātis} — you think, to several people
  \item \textbf{cōgitant} — they think
\end{itemize}

Latin's other everyday verb here is \textbf{putō}, \textquotedblleft{}I reckon, I suppose\textquotedblright{} — lighter, closer to English \textquotedblleft{}I guess.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Cōgitāre} is \emph{co-} (\textquotedblleft{}together\textquotedblright{}) welded onto \emph{agitāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to keep driving about\textquotedblright{} — itself the restless form of \emph{agere}, \textquotedblleft{}to drive, to do.\textquotedblright{} Thinking, to a Roman, is not stillness: it is driving your material together and keeping it in motion.

English took the verb whole in \textbf{cogitate} and \textbf{cogitation}, and took the most quoted sentence in philosophy with it: \emph{cōgitō ergō sum}, \textquotedblleft{}I think, therefore I am\textquotedblright{} — whose second word is the \textbf{sum} you already know.

The engine underneath, \emph{agere}, is one of Latin's great suppliers: \textbf{act}, \textbf{action}, \textbf{agent}, \textbf{agenda} (\textquotedblleft{}things to be driven forward\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{agile}, \textbf{agitate}, \textbf{exact}, and \textbf{navigate} (\emph{nāvis}, \textquotedblleft{}ship,\textquotedblright{} plus \emph{agere}). The root is Proto-Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*ag-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to drive,\textquotedblright{} which in Greek became \emph{ágō} and gave \textbf{pedagogue} (\textquotedblleft{}child-leader\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{demagogue}.

\emph{Putāre} is worth its own paragraph. It first meant \textquotedblleft{}to prune a tree,\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}to settle an account,\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}to consider\textquotedblright{} — and English inherited all three stages: \textbf{amputate}, \textbf{compute} (and its worn-down form \textbf{count}), \textbf{dispute}, \textbf{deputy}, \textbf{impute}, and \textbf{reputation}.

One flag. English \textbf{think} is Germanic, from the root that also gives \textbf{thank} — a thought and a grateful thought. It is not related to \emph{cōgitō}. Nor is \textbf{cognition}, which belongs to \emph{nōscō}, the other knowing verb.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}cōgitō\textquotedblright{} — I think, hard g
  \item \textquotedblleft{}cōgitās, cōgitat\textquotedblright{} — you think, he or she thinks
  \item \textquotedblleft{}cōgitāmus, cōgitātis, cōgitant\textquotedblright{} — we, you all, they
  \item the English relatives — cogitate, agent, agenda, compute
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}I think\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Cōgitō}.) \textquotedblleft{}They think\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Cōgitant}.) What two pieces is the verb built from? (\emph{\textbf{Co-}}, \textquotedblleft{}together,\textquotedblright{} and \emph{agitāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to keep driving about\textquotedblright{}.) Which philosopher's sentence carries it, and which chapter-37 verb closes that sentence? (\emph{\textbf{Cōgitō ergō sum}} — and \textbf{sum}.) Which English word began as \emph{putāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to prune\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Amputate} — and \textbf{compute}, and \textbf{count}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[legō, legere]{legō — reading is picking things up}

\label{lesson:LA-C38-lego}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Cōgitō} drives ideas together. The next verb gathers something more concrete — and it is the single richest word in this book.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: legō — \textquotedblleft{}I read\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Legō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I read}.\textquotedblright{} Its older and wider sense is \textquotedblleft{}I gather, I pick out.\textquotedblright{} The dictionary form is \textbf{legere}. Every \emph{g} is hard and every vowel here is short: \emph{LEH-goh}, \emph{LEH-geh-reh}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{legō} — I read
  \item \textbf{legis} — you read, to one person
  \item \textbf{legit} — he reads, she reads
  \item \textbf{legimus} — we read
  \item \textbf{legitis} — you read, to several people
  \item \textbf{legunt} — they read
\end{itemize}

Reading is the younger meaning, and you can feel how it arrived: you pick the letters up, one after another. A Roman normally did this aloud.

\begin{cousinweb}
The Proto-Indo-European root is \emph{\textbf{*leg-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to gather, to collect.\textquotedblright{}

Straight from \emph{legere} English has \textbf{legible}, \textbf{legend} (\textquotedblleft{}things to be read\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{lectern}, \textbf{lecture}, and — through Old French \emph{leçon}, from \emph{lectiōnem}, \textquotedblleft{}a reading\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{lesson}. A Roman \textbf{legion} was a \emph{legiō}, a levy of men picked out for service.

Prefixed, the verb becomes a machine. \emph{Con-} gives \textbf{collect} (gather together); \emph{sē-} gives \textbf{select} (gather apart); \emph{ē-} gives \textbf{elect} (pick out). \textbf{Neglect} is \emph{nec legere}, \textquotedblleft{}not to pick up.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Elegant} is \emph{ēlegāns} — originally an insult, \textquotedblleft{}too choosy.\textquotedblright{}

Greek inherited the same root as \emph{légō}, \textquotedblleft{}I gather, I speak,\textquotedblright{} and its noun \emph{lógos}, \textquotedblleft{}word, reason.\textquotedblright{} From those come \textbf{logic}, \textbf{catalogue}, \textbf{dialogue}, \textbf{analogy}, \textbf{anthology} (a flower-gathering), and the \emph{-logy} ending on every science you can name.

One caution. Latin \emph{lēx}, \emph{lēgis} (\textquotedblleft{}law\textquotedblright{}) — behind \textbf{legal}, \textbf{legislate}, \textbf{loyal}, and \textbf{privilege} — is often derived from \emph{legere}, \textquotedblleft{}what is read out.\textquotedblright{} That link is \textbf{debated}; treat it as a maybe.

And a false friend: English \textbf{read} is Germanic, from a word meaning \textquotedblleft{}to advise,\textquotedblright{} still visible in \textbf{riddle}. It has nothing to do with \emph{legō}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}legō\textquotedblright{} — I read, hard g
  \item \textquotedblleft{}legis, legit\textquotedblright{} — you read, he or she reads
  \item \textquotedblleft{}legimus, legitis, legunt\textquotedblright{} — we, you all, they
  \item the English relatives — legible, collect, select, elegant
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}I read\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Legō}.) \textquotedblleft{}They read\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Legunt}.) What did the verb mean before it meant \textquotedblleft{}read\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{To gather, to pick out}.) What does \textbf{neglect} literally say? (\emph{\textbf{Nec legere}}, \textquotedblleft{}not to pick up\textquotedblright{}.) Is English \emph{read} a relative? (\textbf{No} — it is Germanic, from a word meaning \textquotedblleft{}to advise\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[intellegō, intellegere]{intellegō — reading between}

\label{lesson:LA-C38-intellego}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Legō} picks things out. Put one small word in front of it and you get the verb behind \textbf{intelligence} itself.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: intellegō — \textquotedblleft{}I understand\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Intellegō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I understand}.\textquotedblright{} The dictionary form is \textbf{intellegere}. It is \emph{legō} with a prefix, so the endings are the ones you have just learned: \emph{in-TEL-leh-goh}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{intellegō} — I understand
  \item \textbf{intellegis} — you understand, to one person
  \item \textbf{intellegit} — he understands, she understands
  \item \textbf{intellegimus} — we understand
  \item \textbf{intellegitis} — you understand, to several people
  \item \textbf{intellegunt} — they understand
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Nōn intellegō} — \textquotedblleft{}I do not understand\textquotedblright{} — is the single most useful sentence in this chapter.

\begin{cousinweb}
The prefix is \emph{inter}, \textquotedblleft{}between, among.\textquotedblright{} Before an \emph{l} it wore down to \emph{intel-}. So \emph{intellegere} is \textbf{to pick out from among}, to read between one thing and another. Latin says outright what English only implies: understanding is discrimination.

The family in English is one of the most familiar in the language: \textbf{intellect}, \textbf{intellectual}, \textbf{intelligent}, \textbf{intelligence}, \textbf{intelligible} and \textbf{unintelligible}, and — borrowed back through Russian — \textbf{intelligentsia}. Military and diplomatic \textbf{intelligence} is the older sense of the noun: information gathered.

There is a spelling puzzle here worth solving. Classical Latin wrote \textbf{intellegō} with an \emph{e}, keeping the vowel of \emph{legō}; later Latin respelled it \emph{intelligō}. English took both, at different dates, which is why \textbf{intellect} keeps the \emph{e} while \textbf{intelligent} carries the \emph{i}. Two spellings, one verb.

\emph{Inter} on its own gave English \textbf{interval}, \textbf{interior}, \textbf{interrupt}, \textbf{international}, and \textbf{interest} — that last one already met as \emph{inter est}, \textquotedblleft{}it is between.\textquotedblright{}

Two flags. Latin had a second word for understanding, \emph{comprehendere}, \textquotedblleft{}to grasp together,\textquotedblright{} which gives \textbf{comprehend} and \textbf{comprehensive}; it is a different image and a different root. And English \textbf{understand} is Germanic, a compound of \emph{under} and \emph{stand} — no connection at all.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}intellegō\textquotedblright{} — I understand
  \item \textquotedblleft{}intellegis, intellegit\textquotedblright{} — you understand, he or she understands
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nōn intellegō\textquotedblright{} — I do not understand
  \item the English relatives — intellect, intelligent, intelligible
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}I understand\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Intellegō}.) \textquotedblleft{}I do not understand\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Nōn intellegō}.) What two pieces is it built from? (\emph{\textbf{Inter}}, \textquotedblleft{}between,\textquotedblright{} and \emph{legere}, \textquotedblleft{}to pick out\textquotedblright{}.) Why does English have both \emph{intellect} and \emph{intelligent}? (\textbf{Two Latin spellings} — classical \emph{intellegō}, later \emph{intelligō}.) Is English \emph{understand} related? (\textbf{No} — it is Germanic.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[scrībō, scrībere]{scrībō — writing began as scratching}

\label{lesson:LA-C38-scribo}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Legō} takes words off a surface and \textbf{intellegō} picks them apart. This verb is the one that put them there.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: scrībō — \textquotedblleft{}I write\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Scrībō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I write}.\textquotedblright{} The dictionary form is \textbf{scrībere}. The \emph{sc} is a plain \emph{sk} and the \emph{ī} is long and held: \emph{SKREE-boh}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{scrībō} — I write
  \item \textbf{scrībis} — you write, to one person
  \item \textbf{scrībit} — he writes, she writes
  \item \textbf{scrībimus} — we write
  \item \textbf{scrībitis} — you write, to several people
  \item \textbf{scrībunt} — they write
\end{itemize}

Note that the endings match \emph{legō} exactly. Two verbs, one pattern.

\begin{cousinweb}
The root is Proto-Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*skreyb\textsuperscript{h}-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to cut, to scratch, to incise.\textquotedblright{} That is not a metaphor. A Roman writing a note pressed a pointed stylus into a wax-coated board; writing \emph{was} scratching, and the verb never forgot it.

The English family is enormous and almost entirely transparent. Bare: \textbf{scribe}, \textbf{scribble}, \textbf{script}, \textbf{scripture}, \textbf{scrivener}. Compounded with a noun: \textbf{manuscript}, \textquotedblleft{}written by hand,\textquotedblright{} from \emph{manus}, the hand. Prefixed with a preposition, the verb runs the whole set — \textbf{describe} (write down), \textbf{prescribe} (write in advance), \textbf{subscribe} (write underneath, which is what signing a document was), \textbf{transcribe} (write across), \textbf{inscribe} (write into), \textbf{circumscribe} (write around), \textbf{proscribe} (post a name publicly, which in Rome meant a death sentence), \textbf{ascribe}, \textbf{conscript}, and \textbf{postscript}.

One quiet survivor: Old English borrowed \emph{scrībere} as \emph{scrīfan}, \textquotedblleft{}to impose a penance in writing,\textquotedblright{} and that gives \textbf{shrive}, \textbf{shrift}, and the Tuesday before Lent, \textbf{Shrove} Tuesday. When somebody gets \textbf{short shrift}, they are being given very little confession time.

Now the honest part. English \textbf{write} is \textbf{not} from this verb. It is Germanic, from a word that also meant \textquotedblleft{}to scratch, to tear\textquotedblright{} — two languages reaching the same image with two different words. \textbf{Scrape} and \textbf{scrub} are likewise Germanic and unrelated, however much they sound the part.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}scrībō\textquotedblright{} — I write, opening sk-
  \item \textquotedblleft{}scrībis, scrībit\textquotedblright{} — you write, he or she writes
  \item \textquotedblleft{}legō, scrībō\textquotedblright{} — I read, I write
  \item the English relatives — scribe, script, describe, manuscript
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}I write\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Scrībō}.) \textquotedblleft{}They write\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Scrībunt}.) What did the root originally mean? (\textbf{To scratch, to incise} — a stylus in wax.) What does \textbf{subscribe} literally say? (\textbf{Write underneath} — to sign.) Is English \emph{write} from this verb? (\textbf{No} — it is Germanic, and happens to mean \textquotedblleft{}scratch\textquotedblright{} too.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[capiō, capere]{capiō — the verb behind English \textquotedblleft{}have\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:LA-C38-capio}



\begin{quote}
When you learned \textbf{habeō}, one thing was left owing: English \emph{have} is not its descendant but belongs to another verb. This is that other verb.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: capiō — \textquotedblleft{}I take\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Capiō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I take},\textquotedblright{} and also \textquotedblleft{}I seize, I catch, I hold.\textquotedblright{} The dictionary form is \textbf{capere}. Both vowels are short and the \emph{c} is hard: \emph{KAH-pee-oh}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{capiō} — I take
  \item \textbf{capis} — you take, to one person
  \item \textbf{capit} — he takes, she takes
  \item \textbf{capimus} — we take
  \item \textbf{capitis} — you take, to several people
  \item \textbf{capiunt} — they take
\end{itemize}

For \textquotedblleft{}take up, take on\textquotedblright{} Latin also used \textbf{sūmō}, \textbf{sūmere}.

\begin{cousinweb}
The root is Proto-Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*keh\textsubscript{2}p-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to grasp.\textquotedblright{} Latin made \emph{capere} of it; the Germanic branch made English \textbf{have} and \textbf{heave}. So \emph{capiō} and \emph{have} really are the same inherited word — the resemblance \emph{habeō} seemed to offer was the false one, and this is the true one.

Plain derivatives: \textbf{capture}, \textbf{captive}, \textbf{captor}, \textbf{caption}, \textbf{capable}, \textbf{capacity}. Prefixed, the \emph{a} often weakens to \emph{i} or \emph{e}, which is what disguises the family: \textbf{accept} and \textbf{except}, \textbf{intercept}, \textbf{anticipate} (\textquotedblleft{}to take beforehand\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{participate} (\emph{pars} plus \emph{capere}, \textquotedblleft{}to take a part\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{occupy}, \textbf{recuperate}, and \textbf{emancipate} — \emph{ex} plus \emph{manus} plus \emph{capere}, \textquotedblleft{}to take out of the hand.\textquotedblright{} Through French the same stem gives \textbf{receive} and \textbf{reception}, \textbf{deceive} and \textbf{deception}, \textbf{conceive} and \textbf{concept}, \textbf{perceive}, and \textbf{susceptible}. Vulgar Latin \emph{captiāre} produced both \textbf{chase} and \textbf{catch}, which are therefore the same word twice.

\textbf{Sūmere} is \emph{sub} plus \emph{emere}, \textquotedblleft{}to take up,\textquotedblright{} and it supplies \textbf{assume}, \textbf{consume}, \textbf{presume}, \textbf{resume}, and \textbf{sumptuous}. \emph{Emere} itself (\textquotedblleft{}to buy\textquotedblright{}) gives \textbf{exempt}, \textbf{redeem}, \textbf{example}, and \textbf{premium}.

Now the trap. Latin \emph{caput}, \textquotedblleft{}head,\textquotedblright{} looks like a member of this family and is not. It is a separate word, and it — not \emph{capere} — gives \textbf{capital}, \textbf{captain}, \textbf{chapter}, \textbf{chief}, and \textbf{cape} the headland.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}capiō\textquotedblright{} — I take, hard c
  \item \textquotedblleft{}capis, capit\textquotedblright{} — you take, he or she takes
  \item \textquotedblleft{}capimus, capitis, capiunt\textquotedblright{} — we, you all, they
  \item the English relatives — capture, accept, receive, concept
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}I take\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Capiō}.) \textquotedblleft{}They take\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Capiunt}.) Which English verb is the same inherited word? (\textbf{Have} — and \textbf{heave}.) What does \textbf{emancipate} literally say? (\textbf{To take out of the hand}.) Do \textbf{capital} and \textbf{captain} belong here? (\textbf{No} — those are from \emph{caput}, \textquotedblleft{}head\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rogō, rogāre]{rogō — asking as reaching straight out}

\label{lesson:LA-C38-rogo}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Dīcō} tells someone something. \textbf{Capiō} takes. This verb is what you do when you want to take and have to ask first.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: rogō — \textquotedblleft{}I ask\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Rogō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I ask}\textquotedblright{} — both asking a question and asking for a thing. The dictionary form is \textbf{rogāre}. The \emph{g} is hard: \emph{ROH-goh}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{rogō} — I ask
  \item \textbf{rogās} — you ask, to one person
  \item \textbf{rogat} — he asks, she asks
  \item \textbf{rogāmus} — we ask
  \item \textbf{rogātis} — you ask, to several people
  \item \textbf{rogant} — they ask
\end{itemize}

Latin's harder-edged partner is \textbf{petō}, \textbf{petere}, \textquotedblleft{}I seek, I aim at, I ask for\textquotedblright{} — asking with an object in view.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Rogāre} is generally traced to the Proto-Indo-European root \emph{\textbf{*reg-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to move in a straight line, to direct\textquotedblright{} — asking pictured as reaching straight out toward somebody. That last step is the standard account rather than a certainty, so hold it loosely. The root itself is a giant: it gives Latin \emph{regō} (\textquotedblleft{}I rule\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{rēx} (\textquotedblleft{}king\textquotedblright{}), hence \textbf{regal}, \textbf{regent}, \textbf{region}, \textbf{direct}, \textbf{correct}, and \textbf{erect}. In the Germanic branch it gives English \textbf{right}; in Sanskrit it gives the \textbf{raja} of \textbf{maharaja}.

From \emph{rogāre} itself English has \textbf{interrogate} (\textquotedblleft{}to ask thoroughly\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{arrogant} and \textbf{arrogate} (\emph{ad-rogāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to claim for oneself\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{abrogate} (\textquotedblleft{}to ask away,\textquotedblright{} to repeal), \textbf{derogatory}, and \textbf{surrogate} (\emph{sub-rogāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to ask in someone's place\textquotedblright{}).

\emph{Petere} runs a second family: \textbf{petition}, \textbf{appetite}, \textbf{compete}, \textbf{repeat}, \textbf{impetus}, \textbf{perpetual}, and \textbf{centripetal}. Its root meant \textquotedblleft{}to fly, to rush,\textquotedblright{} and that is why Latin \emph{penna}, \textquotedblleft{}feather,\textquotedblright{} belongs to it — so \textbf{pen} is a cousin of \emph{petō}, and Greek supplies \textbf{helicopter}, a spiral wing.

Two flags. English \textbf{ask} is Germanic and unrelated. And \textbf{rogue} is often guessed to come from \emph{rogāre}; its origin is genuinely unknown.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}rogō\textquotedblright{} — I ask, hard g
  \item \textquotedblleft{}rogās, rogat\textquotedblright{} — you ask, he or she asks
  \item \textquotedblleft{}rogāmus, rogātis, rogant\textquotedblright{} — we, you all, they
  \item the English relatives — interrogate, arrogant, prerogative
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}I ask\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Rogō}.) \textquotedblleft{}They ask\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Rogant}.) Which root is it generally traced to, and how sure is that? (\emph{\textbf{*reg-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to move in a straight line\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{the standard account, not a certainty}.) Which everyday writing tool comes from \emph{petere}'s family? (\textbf{Pen}, from \emph{penna}, \textquotedblleft{}feather\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[adiuvō, adiuvāre]{adiuvō — the verb inside \textquotedblleft{}aid\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:LA-C38-adiuvo}



\begin{quote}
You can ask now — \textbf{rogō}. This is the verb for what you are hoping the other person will do.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: adiuvō — \textquotedblleft{}I help\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Adiuvō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I help}.\textquotedblright{} The dictionary form is \textbf{adiuvāre}. Two sounds to place: the \emph{i} between vowels is a consonant, said like English \emph{y}, and the \emph{v} is a \emph{w}. So this is \emph{ah-DYOO-woh}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{adiuvō} — I help
  \item \textbf{adiuvās} — you help, to one person
  \item \textbf{adiuvat} — he helps, she helps
  \item \textbf{adiuvāmus} — we help
  \item \textbf{adiuvātis} — you help, to several people
  \item \textbf{adiuvant} — they help
\end{itemize}

The plain verb \textbf{iuvō}, \textbf{iuvāre}, means \textquotedblleft{}to help\textquotedblright{} and also \textquotedblleft{}to please,\textquotedblright{} and \emph{ad-} simply aims it at somebody.

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin built a busier form of \emph{adiuvāre} — \emph{adiūtāre} — and Old French wore that down to \emph{aidier}. English borrowed it as \textbf{aid}, and later took the French agent-noun as \textbf{aide}, which is why \textbf{first aid} and an \textbf{aide-de-camp} both hold this Roman verb without showing a letter of it.

Straight from Latin come \textbf{adjutant} (\emph{adiūtor}, \textquotedblleft{}a helper\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{adjuvant}, the medical term for something given alongside a treatment to help it work. A bishop's assistant is a \textbf{coadjutor}.

Latin's other word for help is \emph{auxilium}, and its family is a surprise. It comes from \emph{augēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to increase\textquotedblright{} — help as an increase of your strength. That verb gives \textbf{auxiliary}, \textbf{augment}, \textbf{auction} (a sale where the price grows), \textbf{author} (\emph{auctor}, one who makes a thing grow), and the month \textbf{August}, for the emperor Augustus, \textquotedblleft{}the increased one.\textquotedblright{} The Germanic branch gives English \textbf{eke} — and a \textbf{nickname} is an \emph{eke-name}, an also-name, with the \emph{n} of \emph{an} stuck to the front.

Two flags, and the first is a real trap. \emph{Iuvō} (\textquotedblleft{}help\textquotedblright{}) is \textbf{not} the source of \textbf{juvenile}. That comes from \emph{iuvenis}, \textquotedblleft{}young,\textquotedblright{} a separate word which also gives \textbf{junior} and \textbf{rejuvenate}. And English \textbf{help} is Germanic, unrelated to any of this.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}adiuvō\textquotedblright{} — I help, with a y and a w inside
  \item \textquotedblleft{}adiuvās, adiuvat\textquotedblright{} — you help, he or she helps
  \item \textquotedblleft{}adiuvāmus, adiuvātis, adiuvant\textquotedblright{} — we, you all, they
  \item the English relatives — aid, aide, adjutant, adjuvant
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}I help\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Adiuvō}.) \textquotedblleft{}They help\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Adiuvant}.) How is the \emph{i} in the middle pronounced? (\textbf{Like English y}.) Which two everyday English words came from it through French? (\textbf{Aid} and \textbf{aide}.) Is \textbf{juvenile} a relative? (\textbf{No} — that is \emph{iuvenis}, \textquotedblleft{}young,\textquotedblright{} a different word.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[amō, amāre]{amō — the eighth verb, and the whole set together}

\label{lesson:LA-C38-amo}



\begin{quote}
Seven verbs so far: to think, to read, to understand, to write, to take, to ask, to help. One remains, and it is the one every Latin class in history has started with.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: amō — \textquotedblleft{}I love\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Amō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I love},\textquotedblright{} and, more mildly, \textquotedblleft{}I like.\textquotedblright{} The dictionary form is \textbf{amāre}. The \emph{a} of \emph{amō} is short, the \emph{ā} of \emph{amās} is long.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{amō} — I love
  \item \textbf{amās} — you love, to one person
  \item \textbf{amat} — he loves, she loves
  \item \textbf{amāmus} — we love
  \item \textbf{amātis} — you love, to several people
  \item \textbf{amant} — they love
\end{itemize}

\emph{Amō, amās, amat} is the oldest teaching formula in the subject. You meet it here in its proper place: as the eighth of eight ordinary verbs.

\begin{cousinweb}
Begin with the honest limit. Every other verb in this chapter walks back to a reconstructed Proto-Indo-European root. \emph{Amāre} does not. It is usually explained as a \textbf{nursery word} — the \emph{am-} sound small children make — which is a respectable account and not a reconstruction. The trail stops earlier here, and saying so is better than inventing a root.

The forward journey makes up for it. \textbf{Amateur} came through French and means \textquotedblleft{}one who loves it\textquotedblright{}; the sneer is a late arrival. Beside it stand \textbf{amatory}, \textbf{amorous}, \textbf{enamoured}, and \textbf{paramour} (\textquotedblleft{}by love\textquotedblright{}). From \emph{amīcus}, \textquotedblleft{}friend,\textquotedblright{} come \textbf{amicable}, \textbf{amity}, and — Spanish being another daughter of Latin — \emph{amigo}. \textbf{Amanda} means \textquotedblleft{}she who is to be loved.\textquotedblright{}

The best of them is upside down. Put the negative \emph{in-} on \emph{amīcus} and you get \emph{inimīcus}, \textquotedblleft{}not-friend\textquotedblright{} — which is English \textbf{enemy}, and \textbf{enmity}, and \textbf{inimical}. The word for an enemy is the word for love with a \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{} in front of it.

Two flags. \textbf{Amen} is Hebrew, borrowed through Greek, and has nothing to do with \emph{amō}. And \textbf{amenable} comes through French \emph{amener}, \textquotedblleft{}to lead to.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}amō, amās, amat\textquotedblright{} — I love, you love, he or she loves
  \item this chapter's eight \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} forms — cōgitō, legō, intellegō, scrībō, capiō, rogō, adiuvō, amō
  \item the eight \textquotedblleft{}he or she\textquotedblright{} forms — cōgitat, legit, intellegit, scrībit, capit, rogat, adiuvat, amat
  \item the English relatives of amāre — amateur, amicable, enemy
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give this chapter's eight \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} forms. (\textbf{Cōgitō, legō, intellegō, scrībō, capiō, rogō, adiuvō, amō}.) Now the eight \textquotedblleft{}he or she\textquotedblright{} forms. (\textbf{Cōgitat, legit, intellegit, scrībit, capit, rogat, adiuvat, amat}.) Why does this lesson name no ancient root? (\textbf{Because \emph{amāre} has none securely reconstructed} — it is taken as a nursery word.) Which English word is \emph{amīcus} with a \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{} on the front? (\textbf{Enemy}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
